message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it, leaving a small lip you can feel underfoot or catch a toe on. It's the most common giveaway of a DIY floor. Long rectangular tiles like your 30 × 60 cm ones are especially prone to it, so see the tips below.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It blends in, and it hides the everyday dirt that turns white or very pale grout grubby within weeks. For extra protection:
- use a stain-resistant or epoxy grout, or
- seal a standard cement-based grout once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tile the whole floor first and fit the toilet on top. You avoid fiddly cuts around the base, you get a neater seal, and you won't have to re-tile if you replace the toilet later. Check that the waste pipe connection will still line up at the new floor height.

## How many boxes?

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24** |
| Plus 10% | 26.4, so **27 tiles** |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes** |

**Why not three boxes?** Three boxes is exactly 24 tiles, leaving no spares at all. One cracked tile or bad cut and you're stuck.

**The spares are worth having.** Four boxes leaves you about 8 spare. That's more than 10%, which is reasonable for a first floor, especially with a staggered layout that needs extra cuts. Keep a couple of leftovers for future repairs.

**Check the boxes before you leave the shop.** Make sure they all have the same batch or shade number, because colour can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names], just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from around [9 am] for a few hours. Sorry for the disruption, and thank you for being so patient with the skip! It should all be finished soon.

## Three tips for a first-time floor

1. **Get the subfloor flat and dry-lay first.**
   - Most problems start with an uneven base, so check it with a long straight edge and level any dips first.
   - Then lay the tiles out without adhesive to plan where the cuts fall. Aim for cut pieces at least half a tile wide around the edges, ideally the less visible ones, rather than thin slivers.
2. **Prevent lippage with long tiles.**
   - Offset each row by **no more than a third** of a tile, not half. Long tiles often bow slightly in the middle, so a half-offset puts the high centre of one tile next to the low ends of its neighbours.
   - A tile levelling clip system is cheap and very beginner-friendly.
3. **Get full adhesive coverage and work in small batches.**
   - Mix only what you can use in about 20–30 minutes.
   - Spread adhesive on the floor with a notched trowel, and butter the back of each tile too.
   - Lift the first couple of tiles to check the back is fully covered. Hollow spots crack later.

**One extra safety note:** cutting porcelain makes fine dust that's harmful to breathe. Use a wet cutter if you can, cut outdoors, and wear a proper dust mask (FFP2 or FFP3) and eye protection.

Good luck. Going slowly and taking time over the dry-lay is most of the battle.
